title: Ashland's Adena mounds
summary: Six conical Adena burial mounds survive in Ashland's Central Park, roughly 15–20 feet across and 4–6 feet high in a slight curve. A 1930s survey said no Kentucky city held…
bodyMarkdown:
In [Ashland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ashland,_Kentucky)'s Central Park, once City Park, six low earthen mounds rise from the lawn, among the few pre-Columbian earthworks left in the city. [Kentucky Historical Marker #921](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/595) notes them as ancient Native American mounds.

The mounds are credited to the [Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture), a people of the Ohio Valley who lived long before the nations that European explorers later met. The Kentucky Historical Society dates the Adena to about 500 BC to AD 100, and notes that mound building may have continued as late as AD 1400. Grokipedia's Ashland article dates these mounds more broadly, to about 1000 BCE to 200 CE.

## Burial, ceremony and memory

The mounds served as burial places, ceremonial sites and landmarks. They grew over time as the dead were buried in layers, one above another, often with ceremonial objects and tools. A mound was a record of a community's dead built up across generations.

That makes them graves as well as monuments. The historical record says the Ashland mounds were opened in the 1870s and were found to hold human remains. Today they are best understood as burial places as well as earthworks.

## A crowded ancient landscape

Mounds once lined the Ohio River in northeastern Kentucky. At least sixteen stood where Ashland is today. A University of Kentucky study in the 1930s said no city in the state held more evidence of prehistoric occupation than Ashland.

Most of those mounds are gone, leveled over the years for buildings and streets. The six survivors are each about 20 feet across and about 6 feet high. Five stand side by side in a line, and the sixth sits slightly offset. Other Kentucky mound sites told on this site include [Dover Mound](/stories/dover-mound-mason-county/), [Wright Mounds](/stories/wright-mounds-montgomery-county/) and the [C and O Mounds at Paintsville](/stories/the-c-and-o-mounds-at-paintsville/).

## Later arrivals

Ashland's written history begins much later. Grokipedia records that the Poage family, Scotch-Irish settlers from Virginia, set up a homestead on the Ohio River in 1786, first known as Poage's Landing. The town that grew there built over much of the older landscape the mounds belonged to.

## Kentucky today

The Central Park mounds stand within a public park and serve, in the Historical Society's words, as evidence that Native people lived and built a culture here long before white settlers arrived. They are also a reminder of what has been lost. Of at least sixteen mounds, six remain, kept by a city that grew up around them.
